explanations.E0011:
# E0011: token where something else belongs

The parser expected one thing and found another. The message names both, with the thing found written as it appears in the source, or as `end of line` or `end of file`.

## Why

Sisu's syntax is small, so the expected thing is nearly always one specific token or kind of name. The message reads as a sentence, such as "expected a binding name, found `=`".

One form has its own message. A `return` or `break` takes everything to its right as its value. When it ends the header of an `if`, a `while`, a `for` or a `match` and a `{` follows, it takes the `{ ... }` of the body as its value, and the body is missing. The report points at the jump. Put the jump in `( )` to give it no value: write `if (o ?? return) {` in place of `if o ?? return {`. The report gives this help only when the `break` stays in the body of its loop. In a loop header the `( )` form is E0082 (see [E0082](E0082.md)), and with no loop it is E0038 (see [E0038](E0038.md)), so the report has no help.

A second form has its own message. A `let ... else` takes no type: remove the `: T`, and the value gives the names their types. A `let` with a pattern and no `else` has a message of its own, "a `let` pattern takes no type", and the same help; it then needs an `else` (see [E0174](E0174.md)).

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let = 1
    print(1)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x = 1
    print(x)
}
```
explanations.W0007:
# W0007: unnecessary `;`

A `;` separates two things on one line that would otherwise need a line break between them: two statements, two fields or methods, two variants, or two `match` arms, as in `let x = 2; print(x * 21)`. Most other `;`s are unnecessary: at the end of a line, at the start of one, right after `{`, before `}` or `else`, at the end of the file, every extra `;` in `;;`, and after a top-level function, class or enum, which needs no separator before the next item. The program still builds. A `;` whose removal would join two lines into one statement stays an error ([E0011](E0011.md)), as at the start of a line before `.f()`, and so does a `;` where something else must come next, as in `let x = ;`.

## Why

A line break already ends a finished statement, so a `;` after one is not needed. Reporting it keeps one way to write a program, and the safe fix removes the `;`. There is no fix for a `;` at the start of a line after an unfinished statement, as after `let x =`. Removing such a `;` by hand can also need a change to the line after it. There is also no fix when the file has a syntax error and the fix would change how the file lexes.

A `;` never changes what a block gives. In `let y = { x; }`, `y` is still `x`: the `;` does not turn the block's value into `unit`, as it would in Rust.

## Broken

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x = 1;
    print(x)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn main() {
    let x = 1
    print(x)
}
```
